title: Impact = Promoting Long-Term Student Flourishing
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Prompted by a reader's question about speaking truth to power, Dave Stuart Jr. steps back to ask what it means for a teacher to have an impact at all. He answers by defining impact as promoting a student's long-term flourishing and, by extension, defining schools as existing for that same end. He unpacks each word: long-term guards against settling for short-lived wins, flourishing is broader than test scores and leaves room for character and calling, and promote casts the teacher as a part-time steward of a garden rather than a hero. He admits the vision is unglamorous compared with Hollywood teacher stories. His case is that it is the only goal durable enough to sustain deep thinking, resilience through hard years, and the teacher's own long-term flourishing.
points: Stuart answers what schools are for with one working definition: a teacher has impact if they promote a student's long-term flourishing.
Choosing long-term over short-term deliberately resists the temptation to count quick signs such as a kid saying they like reading now.
Flourishing is wider than test scores, which are legitimate but incomplete, and it includes plumbers and presidents alike.
The garden image casts the teacher as steward who weeds, waters, and prunes rather than as a dramatic one-year savior.
Pursuing students' long-term good is presented as what sustains teachers through difficult administrators and politics.
quotes: I have had an impact on a student if I promote his or her long-term flourishing. Similarly: Schools exist to promote the long-term flourishing of students.

Short-term impact feels nice — in many cases it feels better than long-term impact because you often get credit for short-term impact and you often don’t for long-term impact — but it’s not what I’m after.

It lets me paint a vision of school for kids that doesn’t exclude anyone because flourishing is about figuring out your calling as a human and then doing those things with all you got. Police officers and plumbers and presidents can all flourish.

Finally, I say “promote” because teaching a group of kids is kind of like getting to be a part-time steward of a bunch of gardens for a year. My job is to promote the flourishing of the kid/garden: I pull weeds, I water, I prune, I fertilize, I provide access to sunlight, all that good stuff that I’m not that good at in real life.
But I think such a vision is the only one that can get us engaged in the kind of deep, sustained thinking that will make us better and stronger and more joyful teachers with each passing year.

It makes us resilient when weathering hard years, difficult administrators, and opportunistic politicians. In short, when we pursue the long-term flourishing of our students, we happen upon our own long-term flourishing as well.
